title: Change a toilet roll on a spring spindle held by one end: seat one end, then steer the free end into the other socket
instruction: Replace the empty toilet roll with the new one: take out the spindle, put the empty tube in the grey tray, slide the new roll onto the spindle and fit the spindle back in the holder.
context: Changing the toilet roll is something almost everyone does at home. The hard part is the refit: with the roll on, only the spindle's two short ends stick out, so it can only be held by one end. One end goes into its socket and the spindle must be kept pushed shorter against that socket while its free end is steered in (the fingers can shorten it first, or the far socket's chamfered edge squeezes it as the end swings in), and only let go once that end has sprung into the second socket. Let go early and the free end swings down and the roll drops. The roll fills most of the gap between the posts, so the spindle must come in at an angle along a narrow path. None of this is in the instruction. Unlike fitting a spring rod that holds itself between two flat walls by friction, the spindle's ends must find two small sockets in a fixed holder, the roll covers the place where one would squeeze it, an old tube must come off first, and success is a roll hanging free in the holder.
setup: Positions are centres, in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases on the table: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. Wall panel (fixed): white painted board 48 cm wide, 1.8 cm thick, 18 cm tall, standing across the table with its front face at x 41.3, on a 7.4 x 44 x 2 cm foot behind it. Toilet-roll holder (fixed to the panel), a chrome two-post holder: a back plate 19 x 6 x 0.8 cm centred on y 0 and two posts 1.7 cm thick and 3.2 cm tall that stand out 8.8 cm from the plate, their inner faces 14.0 cm apart (y +7.0 and -7.0), within the range of real holders that take a spring roller (replacement rollers are sold for openings of about 4 to 6 in). Each inner face has a square socket 16 x 16 mm and 5 mm deep, with a 3 mm 45-degree chamfer on its front edge; the socket centres are at x 33.5, 10.0 cm above the table (7 cm in front of the plate). Chrome friction 0.3. Spindle (loose, 32 g): a standard two-piece telescoping spring roller of light grey plastic: an outer tube 22 mm across (20 g) and an inner tube 19 mm across (12 g) sliding in it on a spring; 15.6 cm tip to tip relaxed, it squeezes up to 3.0 cm shorter; spring 200 N/m (1.2 N when fitted, 6 N fully squeezed; assumed value, not measured); each end is a 12 mm dome; friction 0.3. At the start it is fitted in the holder: 15.0 cm long, both domes at the bottoms of their sockets. Empty tube (loose, 4 g): brown cardboard, 4.5 cm outside, 4.1 cm inside, 10 cm long, hanging on the spindle centred between the posts. New roll (loose, 130 g): a standard household roll of white two-ply toilet paper on a cardboard core, 11.5 cm across and 10.0 cm wide, core hole 4.3 cm; it lies on its side with its axis left to right, centre at x 30.0, y -15.0. Paper friction 0.7. Tray (fixed): grey plastic, 16 cm front to back and 22 cm left to right inside, 3 cm walls 6 mm thick, centred at x 19.0, y 6.0. Nothing else is on the table. The paper's unrolling direction does not matter.
scoring: Measured at the end with a ruler and photos. An end is seated when its tip is at least 3 mm past its post's inner face and inside the 16 mm socket (within 7 mm of its centre front to back and up and down). The new roll is on the spindle when its axis is within 16 mm of the spindle's axis and within 15 degrees of parallel to it, its whole width lies between the spindle's two tips (5 mm tolerance) and its lowest point is at least 1 cm above the table. The empty tube is off the spindle when the same test fails for it. Hands off: no finger pad within 3 cm of the spindle's surface or of the roll's surface. Score 0 if the new roll is not on the spindle or the empty tube is still on it. Otherwise: 1.0 (success, held 1 s): both ends seated, hands off, spindle and roll still (under 1 cm/s; roll turning under 1 rad/s) and the empty tube in the tray (its centre inside the tray walls, at most 4 cm above the table top, still); 0.75: both ends seated and hands off, the tube elsewhere; 0.5: one end seated and hands off; 0.25: any other state with the new roll on the spindle and the tube off it (for example held in the air, or let go with neither end seated but the roll clear of the table).
reset_notes: Put the empty tube back on the spindle, centred, and fit the spindle in the holder (both domes in their sockets); lay the new roll on its side at its marked spot, axis left to right; empty the tray.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The spindle is two tubes on a sliding joint with a linear spring of 30 mm travel. Its spring rate, 200 N/m, is an assumed value, not measured on a real roller. Its tubes collide as 12-sided prisms. The roll is a rigid hollow cylinder (paper compliance is not modelled and the task never squeezes it); the cardboard tube is rigid. Contacts on these parts resist twisting over a 10 mm patch, like real finger pads. The holder and panel are fixed.
